knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6.5, dpi = 110, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

This guide covers the second step of the pipeline: detecting clusters in
a network and interpreting them. It starts from the bibliographic coupling
network of the explanations of the 1970s stagflation built in [the first
guide](from-references-to-networks.html).

```{r}
#| label: network
library(networkflow)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidygraph)

nodes <- subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation")
network <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  method = "similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1
)
```

## What is a cluster?

In a bibliographic coupling network, a group of documents that cite the
same literature, much more among themselves than with the rest of the
network, is the usual operational definition of a *research specialty* or
a *research front* [@morris2008; @boyack2010]. Detecting such groups
without deciding them in advance is the task of *community detection*
[@fortunato2010]. The algorithms differ, but most formalise "more ties
inside than outside" with the **modularity** of a partition
[@newman2004]:

$$
Q = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i,j} \left( A_{ij} - \gamma \frac{k_i k_j}{2m} \right) \delta(c_i, c_j),
$$

with $A_{ij}$ the weight of the edge between documents $i$ and $j$, $k_i$
the total weight of the edges of $i$, $m$ the total weight of the network,
$\delta(c_i, c_j) = 1$ when $i$ and $j$ are in the same cluster, and
$\gamma$ the *resolution*. The term $k_i k_j / 2m$ is the weight expected
between $i$ and $j$ if edges were placed at random given each node's
weight: a partition has a high modularity when clusters gather much more
weight than expected by chance.

## Detecting clusters with Leiden

`add_clusters()` gives access to five algorithms of [`igraph`](https://r.igraph.org/). The Leiden
algorithm [@traag2019] is the default choice of recent bibliometric work.
It improves on Louvain [@blondel2008] by guaranteeing that clusters are
connected, and iterating it keeps refining the partition.

```{r}
#| label: leiden
network <- add_clusters(
  network,
  clustering_method = "leiden",
  objective_function = "modularity",
  resolution = 1,
  seed = 123
)
```

Each document gets a `cluster_leiden` identifier and the share of the
network that its cluster represents (`size_cluster_leiden`). Edges get the
cluster of their two ends, or "00" when they connect two clusters.

```{r}
#| label: leiden-sizes
node_table <- as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")
node_table |>
  count(cluster_leiden, name = "number_of_nodes", sort = TRUE) |>
  rename(community = cluster_leiden)
```

The table gives, for each community (the cluster number, "01" being the
largest), its number of nodes, that is of documents.

### Resolution and the number of clusters

The partition depends on $\gamma$: a higher resolution makes the expected
weight larger and favours more, smaller clusters. Modularity also has a
*resolution limit*: in large networks, it can merge small communities that
are clearly separated [@fortunato2010]. A network can legitimately be
described at several levels of detail, from fields to specialties
[@sjogarde2020], and choosing the resolution is choosing the level of the
study. A scan of resolutions shows how the number of clusters reacts.

Leiden is also stochastic: two runs with different seeds can give
different partitions. A partition we can trust should come back from one
seed to the next. The **adjusted Rand index** (ARI) measures the agreement
between two partitions, from about 0 (no more than chance) to 1
(identical). We run Leiden with ten seeds for each resolution and compare
each partition with the one of the first seed.

```{r}
#| label: resolution-scan
scan <- expand.grid(resolution = seq(0.5, 2, by = 0.25), seed = 1:10)
memberships <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(scan)), function(i) {
  clustered <- add_clusters(
    network,
    clustering_method = "leiden",
    objective_function = "modularity",
    resolution = scan$resolution[i],
    seed = scan$seed[i],
    verbose = FALSE
  )
  as.integer(as_tibble(clustered, active = "nodes")$cluster_leiden)
})
scan$n_clusters <- sapply(memberships, function(m) length(unique(m)))
scan$ari <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(scan)), function(i) {
  reference <- which(scan$resolution == scan$resolution[i] & scan$seed == 1)
  igraph::compare(memberships[[i]], memberships[[reference]], method = "adjusted.rand")
})
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-resolution
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Two panels against the resolution, from 0.5 to 2. Left: the number of
#|   clusters grows from 2 to about 12. Right: the mean adjusted Rand index
#|   between seeds stays close to 1, except a dip to about 0.75 at a
#|   resolution of 1.5.
scan_summary <- aggregate(cbind(n_clusters, ari) ~ resolution, data = scan[scan$seed != 1, ], FUN = mean)
scan_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(resolution = scan_summary$resolution, value = scan_summary$n_clusters, measure = "Mean number of clusters"),
  data.frame(resolution = scan_summary$resolution, value = scan_summary$ari, measure = "Mean ARI with seed 1")
)
ggplot(scan_long, aes(resolution, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = scico::scico(1, palette = "batlow", begin = 0.3), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(colour = scico::scico(1, palette = "batlow", begin = 0.3), size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~measure, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Resolution", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

The number of clusters grows steadily with the resolution, and most
resolutions give partitions that the seed hardly changes. Where the ARI
drops, the algorithm hesitates between partitions of similar quality:
results at that resolution should be read with care. A reasonable
practice is to choose a resolution in a stable range, to report it, and
to check that the clusters a narrative relies on survive at close values
[@traag2013].

### Modularity or CPM?

Leiden can also maximise the **constant Potts model** [@traag2011], which
compares the internal weight $e_c$ of each cluster with $\gamma$ times its
number of pairs: $H = \sum_c [e_c - \gamma \binom{n_c}{2}]$. A cluster is
worth creating when its density exceeds $\gamma$. Unlike modularity, CPM
does not depend on the size of the network, which helps when comparing
clusters across networks of very different sizes, as time windows often
are. But $\gamma$ then lives on the scale of the edge weights:

```{r}
#| label: cpm
edge_weights <- as_tibble(network, active = "edges")$weight
n_documents <- igraph::vcount(network)
density <- sum(edge_weights) / choose(n_documents, 2)
c(smallest = min(edge_weights), median = median(edge_weights), largest = max(edge_weights), density = density)
```

The weights of this network lie between `r signif(min(edge_weights), 2)` and
`r signif(max(edge_weights), 2)`, so that a resolution of 1 asks clusters to be
denser than any pair of documents can be: every document would be its own
cluster. A natural scale for $\gamma$ is the **density** of the network, here
the mean weight over all the pairs of documents, $\bar{w} = \sum_{ik} w_{ik} /
\binom{n}{2} =$ `r signif(density, 2)`. A cluster created with
$\gamma = \bar{w}$ is, on average, as dense as the whole network; with
$\gamma = 2\bar{w}$ or $3\bar{w}$, it must be two or three times denser.
The higher the multiple, the more the clusters split into small, very
cohesive groups:

```{r}
#| label: cpm-density
cpm_scan <- lapply(c(1, 2, 3), function(multiple) {
  clustered <- add_clusters(
    network,
    clustering_method = "leiden",
    objective_function = "CPM",
    resolution = multiple * density,
    seed = 123,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
  sizes <- as_tibble(clustered, active = "nodes") |>
    count(cluster_leiden, name = "number_of_nodes")
  tibble(
    resolution = multiple * density,
    multiple_of_density = multiple,
    clusters = nrow(sizes),
    largest_cluster = max(sizes$number_of_nodes),
    clusters_of_5_nodes_or_more = sum(sizes$number_of_nodes >= 5)
  )
})
bind_rows(cpm_scan)
```

At the density of the network, CPM finds a few sizeable clusters, close to
the readings of modularity, and a tail of small groups; at three times the
density, the largest cluster is much smaller and most documents are in
clusters that are too small to be read. The density gives a starting point,
not a rule: as for modularity, the resolution has to be explored, and the
clusters that a narrative relies on checked at neighbouring values.

## Reading clusters

A cluster is a set of documents with shared references, not an
interpretation. Reading it means going back to its documents: what they
discuss, when, who wrote them, which references they share, and what
distinguishes them from neighbouring clusters [@ding2011].

### Naming clusters with tf-idf

`name_clusters()` gives each cluster a provisional label. With
`method = "tf-idf"`, each cluster is treated as one document made of the
titles of its members, and its label gathers the terms with the highest
tf-idf [@sparckjones1972; @salton1988]: terms frequent in the cluster and
rare in the others,

$$
\text{tf-idf}_{tc} = \frac{n_{tc}}{\sum_u n_{uc}} \times \log\frac{C}{\mathrm{df}_t},
$$

with $n_{tc}$ the count of term $t$ in cluster $c$, $C$ the number of
clusters and $\mathrm{df}_t$ the number of clusters where $t$ appears.

```{r}
#| label: names
network <- name_clusters(
  network,
  method = "tf-idf",
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  text_columns = "source_title",
  nb_terms_label = 3,
  clean_word_method = "lemmatize"
)
node_table <- as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")
clusters <- aggregate(
  as.integer(source_year) ~ cluster_leiden + cluster_label,
  data = node_table,
  FUN = function(year) c(documents = length(year), median_year = median(year))
)
clusters <- do.call(data.frame, clusters)
names(clusters)[3:4] <- c("documents", "median_year")
clusters[order(clusters$median_year), ]
```

The labels and the median years already sketch a history. Clusters of
the late 1970s and early 1980s talk about productivity, oil, wages and
unemployment; clusters centred on the 2000s about the "great inflation"
and policy "rules". This matches the account of @goutsmedt2021: supply
shocks and inflation inertia dominated the first explanations, and a new
literature centred on the role of monetary policy emerged in the 1990s.
Titles are short, and their words are not always informative ("great",
"comment"): labels are only a first guess. `extract_tfidf()` shows more
terms per cluster, and abstracts, when available, give better labels than
titles.

Other methods name a cluster after one of its documents.
`method = "tidygraph_functions"` uses the most central document: the
centrality is any function of [`tidygraph`](https://tidygraph.data-imaginist.com/)
that computes a node measure, given as a call in `tidygraph_function`, and
`label_columns` says which column of the node table makes the label. Here,
each cluster is named after its document with the highest PageRank:

```{r}
#| label: names-central
central <- name_clusters(
  network,
  method = "tidygraph_functions",
  tidygraph_function = tidygraph::centrality_pagerank(),
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  label_columns = c("source_author", "source_year")
)
as_tibble(central, active = "nodes") |>
  distinct(cluster_leiden, cluster_label) |>
  arrange(cluster_leiden)
```

`method = "given_column"` does the same with the highest value of a column
that you provide, such as the number of citations received within the
corpus (`order_by = "node_size"`, with `compute_size = TRUE` in
`build_network()`).

### The role of documents: hubs and bridges

Within a cluster, documents do not play the same role. @guimera2005 propose
to place each node with two measures. The **within-module degree**
compares the weight $\kappa_i$ of the ties of $i$ with its own cluster
$s_i$ with that of the other members,
$z_i = (\kappa_i - \bar{\kappa}_{s_i}) / \sigma_{\kappa_{s_i}}$. The
**participation coefficient** $P_i = 1 - \sum_s (k_{is} / k_i)^2$, with
$k_{is}$ the weight of the ties of $i$ with cluster $s$, is 0 when all
ties stay in one cluster and approaches 1 when they spread evenly across
clusters.

```{r}
#| label: fig-roles
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Scatter plot of the within-module degree z-score against the
#|   participation coefficient for each document, coloured by cluster.
#|   Most documents have z-scores between -2 and 2; a handful of documents
#|   above 2.5 are hubs of their cluster.
network <- add_node_roles(network, module_col = "cluster_leiden")
roles <- as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")
table(roles$role_ga)

ggplot(roles, aes(participation_coeff, within_module_z, colour = cluster_label)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 2.5, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  scico::scale_colour_scico_d(palette = "batlow") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Participation coefficient", y = "Within-module degree (z-score)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2))
```

The shaded area holds the hubs of their cluster ($z \geq 2.5$, the
threshold of Guimerà and Amaral). Documents on the right have ties spread
over several clusters. The two measures combine into seven roles, which
are easier to understand with documents in hand. Here are the documents
that best illustrate the roles that exist in this network:

```{r}
#| label: role-examples
roles |>
  filter(role_ga %in% c("R5 provincial hub", "R6 connector hub", "R3 non-hub connector", "R4 non-hub kinless")) |>
  arrange(role_ga, desc(if_else(grepl("^R[567]", role_ga), within_module_z, participation_coeff))) |>
  group_by(role_ga) |>
  slice_head(n = 3) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(role = role_ga, document = source_label, title = stringr::str_to_sentence(source_title),
            cluster = cluster_label, z = round(within_module_z, 1), participation = round(participation_coeff, 2)) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

How to read them depends on what the nodes and the ties are. Here, nodes
are explanations of the stagflation and ties are shared references:

- A **provincial hub** (R5) is the central document of a literature: it
  shares references with most of the documents of its cluster and with
  hardly any other. Lansing's "Exploring the causes of the great inflation"
  (2000) is one for the cluster on the great inflation, Nordhaus's "Who's
  afraid of a big bad oil shock?" (2007) for the cluster on oil. These are
  the documents to read first to enter a cluster.
- A **connector hub** (R6) is central in its cluster and shares references
  with others too. Pindyck's "Energy price increases and macroeconomic
  policy" (1980) is central in the cluster on productivity, oil and supply
  while its references also belong to other clusters: a document built on
  several literatures that remains well embedded in one.
- A **non-hub connector** (R3) has ties spread over several clusters
  without being central in any: a bridge. Blinder's "The supply-shock
  explanation of the great stagflation revisited" (2013) belongs to the
  cluster on oil but shares references with other clusters: it revisits an
  explanation that earlier documents had built on other bases. In a
  co-citation network, the same role belongs to works used by several
  literatures.
- A **non-hub kinless** document (R4) spreads its ties evenly over all
  clusters. This is not a better bridge than R3: it may be an outlier. The
  only one here, Nitzan's article on "regimes of differential
  accumulation" (2001), shares references with each of five clusters in
  almost equal proportions (17 to 20% of its tie weight in each), and its
  within-module degree is below the average of its own cluster: it is tied
  to everybody a little and to nobody much.

Roles are positions in a network, not judgements on the importance of a
document. Moreover, they depend on the partition. We recompute the roles
for three resolutions of Leiden and follow the five documents above:

```{r}
#| label: role-resolution
resolutions <- c(0.75, 1, 1.5)
by_resolution <- lapply(resolutions, function(resolution) {
  graph <- network |>
    add_clusters(clustering_method = "leiden", objective_function = "modularity",
                 resolution = resolution, seed = 123, verbose = FALSE) |>
    add_node_roles(module_col = "cluster_leiden")
  as_tibble(graph, active = "nodes") |> mutate(resolution = resolution)
})
bind_rows(by_resolution) |>
  group_by(resolution) |>
  summarise(
    clusters = n_distinct(cluster_leiden),
    hubs = sum(role_ga %in% c("R5 provincial hub", "R6 connector hub", "R7 kinless hub")),
    mean_participation = round(mean(participation_coeff), 2)
  ) |>
  as.data.frame()

bind_rows(by_resolution) |>
  filter(source_label %in% c("LANSING-K-2000a", "NORDHAUS-W-2007", "PINDYCK-R-1980",
                             "BLINDER-A-2013", "NITZAN-J-2001")) |>
  select(document = source_label, resolution, role_ga) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = resolution, values_from = role_ga, names_prefix = "resolution ") |>
  as.data.frame()
```

With smaller clusters, more ties cross clusters and the participation
coefficients increase (the mean goes from 0.31 to 0.52). Blinder stays a
connector at the three resolutions, and Lansing a hub, but Pindyck is
only a peripheral document (R2) at 0.75 and a connector hub from 1. A role is therefore a statement about a document *relative to a given
partition*: before interpreting a role in a text, check that it survives a
reasonable change of resolution. Finally, the thresholds of Guimerà and
Amaral were calibrated on metabolic networks. In a network of documents
projected from references, a quarter of the pairs are tied, most documents
have a participation above 0.05, and hubs are rare (three here): the
roles are more useful as a way to find documents to read than as
categories to count.

The same measures mean different things for other nodes: in a co-citation
network, a hub is a classic cited with most of the works of its literature
and a connector a work used by several literatures; for authors coupled
through their references (see [beyond bibliographic coupling](beyond-bibliographic-coupling.html)),
a connector is an author who cites several literatures.

## What comes next

Clusters are easier to read on a map. The [next guide](drawing-networks.html)
shows how to compute the coordinates of the nodes, with several layouts, to
colour the clusters and to draw the network. A single network of the whole
period also mixes literatures that did not coexist: the [last
guide](following-clusters-over-time.html) builds one network per time window
and follows the clusters across windows.
